Protocol Buffers, Distilled

Core Concept

Protobuf is a schema-driven binary serialization format. You define
message structure in .proto files, compile them into code with protoc,
and messages are encoded compactly on the wire. The schema is not
embedded in the data — both sides must know it.

Schema Language (proto3)

    syntax = "proto3";

    message Person {
      string name = 1;
      int32 id = 2;
      repeated string emails = 3;
      Address address = 4;

      enum Type { UNKNOWN = 0; EMPLOYEE = 1; }
      Type type = 5;

      oneof contact {          // union: at most one set
        string phone = 6;
        string pager = 7;
      }

      map<string, int32> scores = 8;
    }

Key rules: - Field numbers (1, 2, 3…) are the wire identity — not names.
Numbers 1–15 encode in 1 byte, so use them for hot fields. Max is
536,870,911; 19000–19999 reserved. - Never reuse or renumber fields. Use
reserved 4, 6; reserved "old_name"; for deleted ones. - Every field is
optional in proto3, with defaults: 0, "", false, empty. Default values
are not serialized — you can’t distinguish “unset” from “zero” unless
you use optional (proto3.15+) or wrapper types. - Enums must have a zero
value (used as default). - repeated = list; map<K,V> = dictionary (sugar
for a repeated key/value message).

Wire Format

Every message is a sequence of tag–value pairs:

tag = (field_number << 3) | wire_type // encoded as varint

Six wire types (two deprecated):

  Type   Name     Used for
  ------ -------- -------------------------------------------------
  0      Varint   int32/64, uint, bool, enum, sint (zigzag)
  1      I64      fixed64, sfixed64, double
  2      LEN      string, bytes, nested messages, packed repeated
  5      I32      fixed32, sfixed32, float

Varints: 7 bits per byte, MSB = continuation flag, little-endian groups.
300 → 0xAC 0x02.

ZigZag (sint32/64): maps signed → unsigned so negatives stay small:
(n << 1) ^ (n >> 31). Plain int32 encodes -1 as 10 bytes; sint32 as 1
byte.

LEN fields: varint length prefix, then raw bytes. Nested messages are
just embedded encoded messages — this makes the format recursive and
enables lazy parsing.

Packed repeated (default in proto3 for scalars): one tag + length +
concatenated values instead of tag-per-element.

Key Properties

-   Not self-describing — bytes are meaningless without the schema.
-   Field order isn’t guaranteed; parsers must accept any order.
    Serialization isn’t canonical — don’t hash/compare encoded bytes.
-   Unknown fields are preserved (proto3.5+), enabling proxies to pass
    through data from newer schemas.
-   Forward/backward compatible if you: only add fields, never change
    numbers/types, keep zero-valued enum first.
-   Last-one-wins: duplicate scalar fields → last value taken (this is
    how merging works).
-   No message framing — the format doesn’t delimit messages; you must
    length-prefix streams yourself.
-   Size limit in practice: ~2 GB; recommended to stay well under a few
    MB per message.

Compatibility-Safe Type Changes

Interchangeable on the wire: int32 ↔ int64 ↔ uint32 ↔ uint64 ↔ bool
(varint family), sint32 ↔ sint64, string ↔ bytes (if valid UTF-8),
fixed32 ↔ sfixed32, fixed64 ↔ sfixed64. Anything else breaks.

One-Line Mental Model

  A protobuf message is a flat stream of
  (field_number, wire_type, value) triples, varint-encoded, where
  meaning lives entirely in the .proto schema and unknown fields are
  skippable by design.

Full spec: https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/
